cluster: origen-own: Origen in his own words (On First Principles and the works that survive in Greek)
summary: Origen's own words can be set beside the later quarrels, but nearly everything in his central book, On First Principles, survives only in Rufinus's Latin, and Rufinus says he smoothed passages he believed heretics had corrupted. Read in that Latin, the Preface lists, among the points plainly handed down through the apostles' preaching, eternal life for the saved and eternal fire for the lost (free will is then called settled), and leaves open where the soul comes from, what the devil and angels are, and what came before and will come after this world. Chapter 1.6.1-2 offers the idea that the end is like the beginning as inquiry rather than definition, and says between its two quoted sentences that punishment according to sins comes before the end; 2.10.4-6 pictures punishment as a physician's fire that mends a dissolved soul; and 3.6 describes a restoration that comes in stages, with the body changed rather than destroyed. Against Celsus, which survives in Greek, says in 6.26 that the full account of punishment is not for the many, and in 8.72 that the Word will one day master every rational soul and abolish evil, while setting aside the question whether evil could ever arise again. Homilies on Jeremiah 20 (also Greek) defends a God who ‘deceives’ for good and speaks of a ‘mystery’ the many must not learn; the lines quoted do not say what the hidden truth about punishment is, though the example just before them (a twice-married woman who has ‘a share in some salvation’) suggests it is milder than the ‘eternal’ punishment the many are told of. The Commentary on Romans (Rufinus's abridged Latin) says in 5.10 that Christ's cross suffices for past, present and future ages and that love, which never fails, will keep the whole creation from falling, and in 6.5 that ‘eternal’ can mean a lifetime or this present age, that eternal life with the Lord has no end, and that even those who rise to shame will have ‘eternal life’, though not in Christ Jesus. Where Rufinus and the hostile Greek in Justinian's Letter to Menas (543) differ, as at 1.2.13, editors split: Koetschau (and so Butterworth, who translated his text) trust the Greek and print a mixed text, while Crouzel-Simonetti and Behr print Rufinus and move the Greek aside. Scholars read the lines in different directions: Ramelli (through Nemes, Sytsma and Kimel, and in her own review of Arruzza), Hannen and Heide find a restoration that is taught; Crouzel (through Sytsma and Hannen) calls it a hope that cannot be certain without denying freedom; Batiffol finds Origen teaching it as a rule but at times reluctant to decide and not wishing it preached to all; McClymond doubts both Rufinus's Latin and Ramelli's defence; and Martens reads the Preface as making the church's rule of faith the test. Caution on method: the Latin of On First Principles and of the Romans commentary below is Migne's (Patrologia Graeca 11 and 14, Delarue's text) read from OCR page transcriptions, not Koetschau's or Hammond Bammel's critical text, which could not be reached.

passages.title: The rule of faith, and what the church's preaching leaves open (On First Principles, Preface 4-10)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles (Peri Archon, De principiis), Preface 4-10, in Rufinus's Latin translation
passages.date: Origen's Greek: written in Alexandria, before c. 230 (exact date disputed). Rufinus's Latin: 397-98.
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; the Greek of the Preface is lost)
passages.original: (4) Species vero eorum quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo quod unus Deus est qui omnia creavit atque composuit … Tum deinde honore ac dignitate Patri ac Filio sociatum tradiderunt Spiritum sanctum. In hoc non jam manifeste discernitur, utrum natus an innatus vel Filius etiam Dei ipse habendus sit, necne. Sed inquirenda jam ista pro viribus sunt de sacra Scriptura, et sagaci perquisitione investiganda. (5) Post haec jam quod anima substantiam vitamque habens propriam, cum ex hoc mundo discesserit, pro suis meritis dispensabitur, sive vitae aeternae ac beatitudinis haereditate potitura, si hoc ei sua gesta praestiterint; sive igni aeterno ac suppliciis mancipanda … Est et illud definitum in ecclesiastica praedicatione, omnem animam rationabilem esse liberi arbitrii et voluntatis … De anima vero utrum ex seminis traduce ducatur, ita ut ratio ipsius vel substantia inserta ipsis seminibus corporalibus habeatur, an vero aliud habeat initium: et hoc ipsum initium si genitum est, aut non genitum: vel certe si extrinsecus corpori inditur, necne: non satis manifesta praedicatione distinguitur. (6) De diabolo et angelis ejus contrariisque virtutibus ecclesiastica praedicatio docuit, quoniam sunt quidem haec; quae autem sint, aut quomodo sint, non satis clare exposuit. (7) … Quid tamen ante hunc mundum fuerit, aut quid post mundum erit, jam non pro manifesto multis innotuit. (10) … De sole autem et luna et stellis utrum animantia sint, an sine anima, manifeste non traditur.
passages.edition: Standard critical edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke 5: De principiis (Peri archon), Griechische christliche Schriftsteller (GCS) 22 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1913), Praefatio 4-10; page not confirmed. Modern editions with translation: H. Crouzel and M. Simonetti, Origene: Traite des principes, Sources Chretiennes (SC) 252 (Paris: Cerf, 1978); J. Behr, Origen: On First Principles, Oxford Early Christian Texts (Oxford: OUP, 2017). Neither was opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau (the archive.org scan of GCS 22 could not be read in sections; see the unverified list). Checked against the Latin of Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11 (Paris, 1857; Delarue's text), cols. 117-122, from OCR page transcriptions: Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica (teste/PG011, second batch, pages 063-064) and OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11 (hvd.32044024345175_ocr, page 066), compared with two further OCR copies of the same page for section 4. The ligatures ae and oe are written out. The spelling (j, haereditas) is Migne's, not Koetschau's. One clause in section 5 (‘si in hoc eam scelerum culpa … ’) was left out because the OCR gave a doubtful verb. Second pass (fact-check): every word of the Latin was found again in those OCR pages once hyphenated line-ends were joined and the ligatures written out; the only differences were OCR damage. Koetschau's text was still not reachable.
passages.english: (4) The main points of what is plainly handed down through the apostles' preaching are these. First, that there is one God, who created and arranged all things … Then they handed down that the Holy Spirit is joined with the Father and the Son in honour and dignity. About this it is not yet clearly distinguished whether he is born or unborn, or whether he is also to be counted a Son of God, or not. But these matters must be inquired into, as far as we are able, from the sacred Scripture, and tracked down by a keen search. (5) Next, that the soul, having its own substance and life, when it leaves this world will be dealt with according to its merits: either to inherit eternal life and blessedness, if its deeds have earned it, or to be handed over to eternal fire and punishments … It is also settled in the church's preaching that every rational soul has free choice and will … But as to the soul, whether it is passed on by descent, so that its principle or substance is contained in the bodily seeds themselves, or whether it has some other beginning, and whether that beginning is itself begotten or unbegotten, or again whether it is put into the body from outside or not: this is not distinguished with sufficient clarity in the preaching. (6) About the devil and his angels and the opposing powers, the church's preaching has taught that they exist; what they are or how they exist it has not set out clearly enough. (7) … But what there was before this world, or what will be after the world, has not yet become plain to many. (10) … As to the sun, moon and stars, whether they are living beings or without soul, nothing is plainly handed down.
passages.english_source: Own translation. For comparison: F. Crombie in the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885, public domain); G. W. Butterworth (1936); J. Behr (2017). None was opened for this entry. Contested renderings: ‘aeternus’ (eternal or age-long) in ‘igni aeterno’ and ‘vita aeterna’; ‘natus an innatus’ (born/unborn, or begotten/unbegotten, or made/unmade, see the note); ‘praedicatio ecclesiastica’ (the church's preaching, proclamation or teaching).
passages.why_it_matters: This is Origen's own list of what the church's preaching has settled and what it has not. In Rufinus's Latin, eternal fire (‘igni aeterno’) stands on the list of points ‘plainly handed down’ through the apostles' preaching (section 4 introduces the list, section 5 gives the soul's reward and punishment), and free will is then added as ‘settled’ (definitum); what Greek word lies behind ‘aeterno’ is not known. The origin of the soul, the nature of the devil and angels, and the time before and after this world are not on it. Later condemnations (the 553 anathemas) treat some of those open questions, pre-existence above all, as heresy, so the argument is over whether Origen offered them as inquiry or taught them as doctrine.
passages.textual_notes: Migne's apparatus (cols. 117-120) records the manuscript readings Delarue preferred over the earlier printed editions. The most telling is note 51: where Rufinus has ‘natus an innatus’ (begotten or unbegotten) for the Spirit, Jerome's Letter 94 (= 124) to Avitus renders it ‘factus an infectus’ (made or unmade); Delarue reasons that Jerome read the Greek with one nu (genetos/agenetos, created/uncreated) and Rufinus with two (gennetos/agennetos, begotten/unbegotten). That one-letter difference decides whether Origen is asking if the Spirit is a creature. Note 55: the manuscripts read ‘extrinsecus corpori inditur’ (put in from outside) where some earlier editions had ‘intrinsecus’. Notes 53-54: a clause of section 5 is also found in the Apology for Origen by Pamphilus (in Rufinus's Latin), which is one of the few controls on Rufinus. Rufinus's own preface (Jerome Letter 80) says he removed or corrected passages he thought heretics had inserted; the c400 file in this survey has that text. Section numbers follow Migne/Delarue; they agree with Koetschau's in the Preface as far as I could tell, not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Michael McClymond
readings.work: ‘Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus: A Review of Ilaria Ramelli’s The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis’, Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), pp. 815, 818-19 and n. 12
readings.position: Says it was “not Origen’s exegesis but his ‘dogmatizing’—and that of his followers—that stirred controversy” (p. 815), naming pre-existent souls and universal salvation among the teachings of On First Principles at issue. He also says that modern scholars have not accepted Rufinus’s theory that heretics interpolated the text, that Rufinus “tampered with the textual evidence”, and that his Latin is “skewed, inaccurate” (pp. 818-19, n. 12). He does not say, in the lines I could read, whether the charge of dogmatizing was fair.
readings.side: holds that Origen’s dogmatizing, not his exegesis, caused the controversy; distrusts Rufinus’s text and Ramelli’s defence

readings.scholar: Mark Edwards and Panayiotis Tzamalikos (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Edwards, Origen against Plato (2002); Tzamalikos, Origen: Philosophy of History and Eschatology (Brill, 2007); as reported in Martens’s review of Mark Scott, Journey Back to God, Marginalia Review of Books
readings.position: Martens says Scott should have answered Edwards and Tzamalikos, “both of whom deny Origen ever taught” the pre-existence of souls. The review does not tie their argument to the Preface by name; it matters here because Preface 7 leaves open what there was before this world.
readings.side: Origen did not teach pre-existence, so what the 553 text condemns is not his doctrine

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 124 to Avitus, 124.4.5 (Hilberg, CSEL 56, p. 100 l. 26 to p. 101 l. 4); Latin text as recorded in this survey’s c400 file
readings.position: Quotes Origen’s own plea that such ideas are “not dogmas but only questions raised and thrown out” (“non sint dogmata sed quaesita tantum atque proiecta”), and attacks them anyway. Hilberg’s source notes, as recorded in the c400 file, link the sentence to On First Principles 1.8.4, not to the Preface.
readings.side: ancient hostile reader who reports the disclaimer and judges the doctrine anyway

readings.scholar: Peter Martens
readings.work: Review of Mark S. M. Scott, Journey Back to God: Origen on the Problem of Evil, Marginalia Review of Books
readings.position: Cites the Preface to Book 1 against Scott’s claim that Origen valued “internal assimilation of doctrine” over assent to propositions: Origen there “insists that the index of orthodoxy was assent to the church’s rule of faith”.
readings.side: reads the Preface as making assent to the church’s rule of faith the test of orthodoxy

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 24 and n. 49 (Crouzel, pp. 163-168)
readings.position: Hannen cites Crouzel for treating On First Principles as “research theology”. This is a judgement about the book as a whole, not about the Preface by name.
readings.side: reads the speculative parts of the book as inquiry, not as fixed doctrine

passages.title: ‘The end is always like the beginning’ (On First Principles 1.6.1-2)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 1.6.1-2 (Rufinus's Latin); the sentence is cited as 1.6.2
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; no Greek survives for these lines)
passages.original: (1.6.1) … Quae quidem a nobis etiam cum magno metu et cautela dicuntur, discutientibus magis et pertractantibus quam pro certo ac definito statuentibus. … Nunc autem disputandi specie magis quam definiendi, prout possumus, exercemur. Finis ergo mundi et consummatio dabitur, cum unusquisque pro merito peccatorum etiam poenis subjicietur; quod tempus Deus solus agnoscit, quando unusquisque quod meretur expendet. In unum sane finem putamus quod bonitas Dei per Christum suum universam revocet creaturam, subactis et subditis etiam inimicis. (1.6.2) Talem igitur finem videntes, cum omnes inimici subjecti erunt Christo, et cum novissimus inimicus destruetur mors, et cum tradetur a Christo cui omnia subjecta sunt, regnum Deo Patri, ab isto, inquam, tali fine rerum contemplemur initia. Semper enim similis est finis initiis; et ideo sicut unus omnium finis, ita unum omnium intelligi debet initium; et sicut multorum unus finis, ita ab uno initio multae differentiae ac varietates, quae rursum per bonitatem Dei et subjectionem Christi, atque unitatem Spiritus sancti in unum finem qui sit initio similis revocantur.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913); Hilberg's source notes (as quoted in the c400 file) put 1.6.2-3 at pp. 81-83, which I did not check myself. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978); Behr (OUP, 2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 165-166 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, first batch, page 087), which separates the main text from Delarue's notes. Ligatures written out; no other change. Second pass: all other words re-found in the same page (after joining hyphenated line-ends); Delarue’s notes 51, 54, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62 and 64 read as described.
passages.english: (1.6.1) … We say these things with great fear and caution, discussing and weighing them rather than laying them down as certain and defined. … Here, as well as we can, we are exercising ourselves in the manner of a debate rather than of a definition. The end and consummation of the world will be given when each person is made subject to punishments in proportion to his sins; God alone knows that time, when each will pay what he deserves. We think that the goodness of God, through his Christ, will call back his whole creation into one end, with even the enemies conquered and subdued. (1.6.2) Seeing such an end, when all enemies shall be subject to Christ, when the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed, and when the kingdom is handed over by Christ, to whom all things are subject, to God the Father: from that end, I say, let us consider the beginnings. For the end is always like the beginnings; and therefore, as we must understand one end of all things, so also one beginning of all; and as there is one end of many, so from one beginning come many differences and varieties, which are in turn called back, through God's goodness, the subjection of Christ and the unity of the Holy Spirit, into one end that is like the beginning.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘finis’ (end, goal or purpose); ‘revocet’ and ‘revocantur’ (call back, recall, restore; the Greek verb behind them is not preserved); ‘putamus’ (we think, i.e. a hedged claim); ‘initiis’ is plural (beginnings); ‘universam creaturam’ (the whole creation, which may or may not include the devil and demons: Rufinus and Jerome disagree).
passages.why_it_matters: These lines are the source of the famous sentence that the end is like the beginning, which the 553 fifteen anathemas echo (‘the end and the beginning shall be alike’). The argument is over what ‘beginning’ means (a state of bodiless pre-existent minds, or only God's original purpose) and how firmly the surrounding words claim it: Origen frames it as discussion ‘rather than definition’.
passages.textual_notes: Delarue marks the key sentences ‘Cautè lege’ (read with caution) in notes 57, 60, 61 and 64 (note 58, on ‘In unum sane finem putamus’, only sends the reader to Huet’s Origeniana, 2.11.9 and 2.35.30) and, in note 62, says that Jerome (Letter 94 = 124 to Avitus) attacks this very place. Note 51: some earlier editions had ‘videtur esse judicium’ where the manuscripts have ‘videtur indicium’ (a sign). Note 54: the manuscripts read ‘fidem ecclesiasticam’ where earlier editions had ‘catholicam’. The word ‘putamus’ (we think) in ‘In unum sane finem putamus’ is Rufinus's; if his Greek had a stronger verb, this is where he could have softened it, which is the kind of question the c400 file raises about 1.6.3.

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 94 (also numbered 124) to Avitus, quoted in Delarue's note 62 at PG 11 col. 166
readings.position: Reads 1.6.2 as teaching an endless cycle: ‘the beginning is born again from the end and the end from the beginning; and so all things change, so that he who is now a man could become a demon in another world; and a demon who has acted rather carelessly is banished into coarser bodies, that is, becomes a man. So he mixes everything up, so that from an angel the devil can come to be and the devil return to being an angel.’ (Own translation of the Latin as printed in the note.)
readings.side: ancient hostile reader: takes ‘end like beginning’ to mean endless cycling between angel, man and devil

readings.scholar: Michael McClymond
readings.work: ‘Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus’, Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), p. 824 n. 24
readings.position: Quotes ‘the end is always like the beginning’ to show that Origen's apokatastasis (restoration of all things) is a return to a state that existed before, and contrasts this with Gregory of Nyssa's rejection of pre-existent souls. His wider charge is that Ramelli does not keep Origen apart from Gregory of Nyssa.
readings.side: reads the sentence as tied to Origen's pre-existence, so not a model for Nyssa's universalism

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), pp. 197-199 and n. 13
readings.position: Quotes 1.6.1 in an English translation (“the goodness of God through Christ will restore his entire creation to one end”, p. 198) and reads Origen’s punishments as correction rather than retribution (pp. 198-199). In n. 13 (p. 197) he adds that Origen takes a more cautious line on the devil: in a letter he denies teaching the devil’s redemption, but in his dialogue with Candidus he admits it as a real possibility (he cites Jennifer Heckart, Union Seminary Quarterly Review 60).
readings.side: reads 1.6 as teaching restoration of creation, with the devil’s case left open

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 24 and nn. 49-50 (Crouzel, pp. 163-168)
readings.position: Hannen cites Crouzel for calling On First Principles “research theology”. The words “in the manner rather of an investigation and discussion, than in that of fixed and certain decision” are Hannen quoting Origen in an English translation, cited to 1.6.1 (n. 50), not Crouzel’s own words.
readings.side: reads 1.6 as inquiry that does not claim to define

passages.title: Punishment as a physician's fire (On First Principles 2.10.4-6)
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; no Greek survives for these sections)
passages.original: (2.10.4) … ita anima cum multitudinem malorum operum et abundantiam in se congregaverit peccatorum, competenti tempore omnis illa malorum congregatio effervescit ad supplicium, atque inflammatur ad poenas; … tunc et ipsa conscientia propriis stimulis agitatur atque compungitur, et sui ipsa efficitur accusatrix et testis. … (2.10.5) … Quae animae dissolutio atque divulsio cum adhibiti ignis ratione fuerit explorata, sine dubio ad firmiorem sui compaginem instaurationemque solidatur. (2.10.6) Multa sunt etiam alia quae nos latent, quae illi soli cognita sunt, qui est medicus animarum nostrarum. … quanto magis intelligendum est et hunc medicum nostrum Deum volentem diluere vitia animarum nostrarum, quae ex peccatorum et scelerum diversitate collegerant, ut huiuscemodi poenalibus curis, insuper etiam ignis inferre supplicium his qui sanitatem animae perdiderunt? … Ex quo utique intelligitur quod furor vindictae Dei ad purgationem proficit animarum. Quoniam autem et ea poena quae per ignem inferri dicitur, pro adjutorio intelligitur adhiberi, Isaias docet …
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), Book 2 chapter 10; page not confirmed. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978), where Sytsma places 2.10.8 at pp. 392-394; Behr (2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 237-240 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, first batch, pages 122-124). The wording ‘ut huiuscemodi poenalibus curis, insuper etiam ignis inferre supplicium’ is copied as the scan has it; the construction is awkward and the Latin may differ in Koetschau (ignis for igni?). Ligatures written out.
passages.english: (2.10.4) … So when the soul has gathered into itself a great mass of evil deeds and an abundance of sins, at the fitting time that whole accumulation of evils boils up into punishment and is set on fire for penalties; … then the conscience itself is stirred and pricked by its own goads and becomes its own accuser and witness. … (2.10.5) … When this dissolution and tearing apart of the soul has been tested by the working of the fire applied to it, it is without doubt rebuilt into a firmer structure and made whole. (2.10.6) There are many other things that escape us, known only to him who is the physician of our souls. … How much more must we understand that this physician of ours, God, wishing to wash out the vices of our souls, which they had gathered from the variety of sins and crimes, uses such penal cures and, over and above them, brings the punishment of fire on those who have lost the soul's health? … From this it is understood that the fury of God's vengeance serves the purging of souls. And that the punishment said to be brought by fire is understood to be applied as a help, Isaiah teaches …
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘furor vindictae’ (fury or anger of vengeance; the Latin may reflect Greek orge); ‘purgationem’ (purging or purification); ‘ignem’ is the fire of punishment but Origen treats it as the soul's own passions in 2.10.4-5, so ‘fire’ is partly figurative.
passages.why_it_matters: Here Origen most clearly describes punishment after death as medicine: the fire is the soul's own inflamed sins, and God uses it to rebuild what has come apart. Whether that means punishment ends (and so restoration) is the question the sixth-century anathema on ‘temporary punishment’ answers with a condemnation; Origen himself in these sections does not say how long it lasts.
passages.textual_notes: Adjacent and disputed: at 2.10.8 Koetschau supplied, from Jerome and Justinian, a sentence he thought Rufinus had omitted: ‘There is a resurrection of the dead, and there is punishment, but not everlasting’ (reported by Sytsma, p. 11 n. 23, citing Butterworth p. 146 and SC 252 pp. 392-394). Sections 4-6 are Rufinus's Latin without a Greek control. In 2.10.6 Migne's text (as the scan has it) reads ‘ut huiuscemodi poenalibus curis’; I translate as if ‘uti’ (to use), which the sense seems to need, and have not seen a critical edition. Delarue's section numbers are used here; Koetschau's numbering agrees as far as I can tell, not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 25 and nn. 59-62
readings.position: Reads Origen’s doctrine of punishment as remedial, like a physician’s treatment (he quotes “God is the physician of our souls”, n. 62, citing 2.10.6). He also quotes “for all wicked men, and for demons, too, punishment has an end”, but his n. 59 cites that to 2.10.3, and I could not match the sentence to the lines quoted here; it may come from Koetschau’s inserted sentence at 2.10.8. On the devil he notes Origen contradicts himself, citing Holliday and Heckart (nn. 60-61).
readings.side: reads 2.10 as teaching limited, curative punishment ending in restoration

readings.scholar: Paul Koetschau (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), p. 11 n. 23, on Koetschau’s text of 2.10.8
readings.position: Sytsma writes that Koetschau believes Rufinus omits at 2.10.8 the line “There is a resurrection of the dead, and there is punishment, but not everlasting” (citing Butterworth p. 146 and SC 252, pp. 392-394), and so restored it.
readings.side: treats Rufinus as having softened the passage on the end of punishment

readings.scholar: Pierre Batiffol
readings.work: ‘Apocatastasis’, Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (1907)
readings.position: Says Origen “seems at times reluctant to decide” on the eternity of punishment but that “elsewhere, on the other hand, and as a rule, Origen teaches the apokatastasis”. This is a general judgement on Origen, not a reading of 2.10 by section.
readings.side: reads Origen as usually teaching restoration, but hesitating on the duration of punishment

passages.title: God ‘all in all’: restoration in stages, and the body changed, not destroyed (On First Principles 3.6)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 3.6.1, 3.6.3 and 3.6.6 (Rufinus's Latin), with a Greek fragment at 3.6.3 preserved by Justinian
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus), with one Greek fragment (Justinian's Letter to Menas, 543)
passages.original: (3.6.1) … Igitur summum bonum ad quod natura rationabilis universa festinat, quod etiam finis omnium dicitur, a quamplurimis etiam philosophorum hoc modo terminatur, quia summum bonum sit, prout possibile est, similem fieri Deo. … (3.6.3) … quod non solum in omnibus esse dicitur Deus, sed etiam omnia in omnibus. Quae sint ergo ista omnia quae Deus futurus sit in omnibus, requiramus. … (3.6.6) … cum sensim et per singulos emendatio fuerit et correctio prosecuta, praecurrentibus aliis et velociori cursu ad summa tendentibus, aliis vero proximo quoque spatio insequentibus, tum deinde aliis longe posterius, et sic per multos et innumeros ordines proficientium ac Deo se ex inimicis reconciliantium pervenitur usque ad novissimum inimicum qui dicitur mors, ut etiam ipse destruatur ne ultra sit inimicus. Cum ergo restitutae fuerint omnes rationabiles animae in huiuscemodi statum, tunc natura etiam huius corporis nostri in spiritalis corporis gloriam perducetur. … non aliud corpus est quo nunc in ignobilitate et in corruptione et infirmitate utimur, et aliud erit illud quo in incorruptione, et in virtute, et in gloria utemur; sed hoc idem abjectis his infirmitatibus in quibus nunc est, in gloriam transmutabitur spiritale effectum, ut quod fuit indignitatis vas, hoc ipsum expurgatum fiat vas honoris et beatitudinis habitaculum.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), Book 3 chapter 6; page not confirmed. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 268 (1980; volume number from memory); Behr (OUP, 2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 333-340 (Delarue's text), from OCR page transcriptions in OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11: mdp.39015013266690_ocr pages 180, 181, 183 and hvd.32044024345175_ocr pages 172, 175. Two-column pages were read in several copies and only contiguous lines are quoted. The OCR drops large parts of some pages, so section 3.6.5 (the passage on the destruction of the last enemy, which I recall says that what is destroyed is the enemy's will, not its substance) was NOT obtained; 3.6.6 is quoted instead for the same point. Ligatures written out; ‘restitutae’ and ‘abjectis’ corrected from OCR slips (‘restitutte’, ‘abjectis’ already as printed).
passages.english: (3.6.1) … The highest good, toward which all rational nature hurries, which is also called the end of all things, is defined by very many of the philosophers too in this way: that the highest good is to become like God, as far as is possible. … (3.6.3) … that God is said to be not only in all things but also all things in all. Let us ask, then, what those ‘all things’ are that God will be in all. … (3.6.6) … when, little by little and one by one, amendment and correction have gone forward — some running ahead and reaching the heights at a swifter pace, others following close behind, others again much later — and so through many and countless ranks of those advancing and being reconciled to God from being enemies, one comes at last to the last enemy, which is called death, so that even he is destroyed and is no longer an enemy. When, then, all rational souls have been restored to such a state, then the nature of this body of ours too will be carried up into the glory of the spiritual body. … It is not one body that we now use in dishonour, corruption and weakness, and another that we shall use in incorruption, power and glory; rather this same body, its present weaknesses cast off, will be changed into glory, made spiritual, so that what was a vessel of dishonour, once purified, becomes a vessel of honour and a dwelling of blessedness.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘restitutae’ (restored; the Greek is apokatastasis-language, so ‘restoration’ and ‘universal salvation’ are the two usual glosses); ‘destruatur’ (destroyed, abolished or put out of action: the point is whether the enemy ceases to exist or ceases to be an enemy); ‘Deus omnia in omnibus’ (1 Cor 15:28: God all in all, or God everything in everyone); ‘rationabiles animae’ (rational souls or rational beings).
passages.why_it_matters: This chapter is Origen’s fullest account of the end. Three points are in dispute between readers: whether ‘all in all’ includes the wicked and the devil, whether the stages of amendment end with every rational being restored, and whether bodies belong to the final state. Rufinus’s Latin has this body changed into a spiritual body, not abolished; the Greek fragment Justinian quotes in his Letter to Menas (see the textual notes) says God does not become ‘all in all’ in bodies, which by their own nature are lifeless.
passages.textual_notes: Section numbers are Migne/Delarue's. At 3.6.3 Migne prints, between Rufinus's sentences, a Greek fragment taken from the end of Justinian's Letter to Menas and, beside it, Delarue's own Latin rendering of that Greek: ‘Λεγομένου τοῦ Θεοῦ πάντα γενέσθαι ἐν πᾶσιν, ὥσπερ οὐ δυνάμεθα κακίαν καταλιπεῖν, οὔτε Θεὸς πάντα γίνεται ἐν πᾶσιν, οὐδὲ ἄλογα ζῶα, ἵνα μὴ καὶ ἐν κακίᾳ ὁ Θεὸς γίνηται, καὶ ἐν ἀλόγοις ζώοις· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ ἄψυχα, ἵνα μὴ καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεός, ὅτε πάντα γίνεται. Οὕτως οὐδὲ σώματα, ἅτινα τῇ ἰδίᾳ φύσει ἄψυχά ἐστιν.’ Roughly: when it is said that God will become all in all, God does not become all in all irrational animals, lest God also come to be in wickedness, nor in inanimate things, nor in bodies, which by their own nature are inanimate. The first clause is obscure in the scan and in Delarue's rendering and I would not rest an argument on my reading of it. (OCR slips fixed: ὲν to ἐν, ἇψυχα to ἄψυχα, ἆτινα to ἅτινα; the scan has a line-break hyphen inside Λεγομένου and ἄλογοις.) This Greek says something Rufinus's Latin does not say, which is the editions problem in miniature (see the next entry on 1.2.13). Delarue's note 44 records that the words ‘quod non solum in omnibus esse dicitur Deus, sed etiam omnia in omnibus’ were missing from earlier printed editions and supplied from the manuscripts. Note 57: ‘quod etiam finis’ (manuscripts) against ‘quae etiam finis’ (editions). Note 52, to a sentence a little after the lines quoted (about 3.6.5, not obtained), says the manuscripts have ‘namque’ and lack the words ‘id est diabolus’ after ‘inimicus’ that the earlier printed editions add: an explicit gloss identifying the last enemy with the devil.

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), pp. 196-199 (citing 3.6.3) and n. 15
readings.position: Reads 3.6 as saying evil is abolished, not substance: apokatastasis is the return of all rational creatures and the dissolving of every contrast between good and evil (‘there will no longer be any contrast of good and evil, since evil nowhere exists’, p. 197), and he thinks the devil's redemption follows from Origen's ontology. For a detailed treatment he sends readers to Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (2013), pp. 144-156, without saying whether he agrees.
readings.side: reads 3.6 as teaching restoration of all rational creatures, evil ending because it has no being

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 25 and nn. 56, 58
readings.position: Says restoration comes through “word, reason, and doctrine”, which he cites to 3.6.8 (n. 56, a section not quoted here). In the next sentence he argues that human freedom and divine determinism do not conflict, citing MacDonald (p. 33) and Ramelli (p. 167) in n. 58.
readings.side: reads 3.6 as universal restoration that respects freedom

readings.scholar: Jean Danielou (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), pp. 20-21 and nn. 41, 45, citing Danielou (English translation, 1955, p. 289)
readings.position: Sytsma quotes Danielou on “the metaphysical necessity of the ultimate elimination of evil” (p. 20) and says his analysis ended in “a certain incoherence” in Origen’s theology (p. 21), because that necessity pulls against the creature’s freedom. The report is about Origen’s system, not 3.6 alone.
readings.side: doubts that the strict argument for the end of evil fits the stress on freedom

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Brill, 2013), cited in Sytsma, pp. 31-32 and nn. 79, 83, 84
readings.position: Sytsma reports Ramelli grounding the end of evil in its non-subsistence: “Providence does not force rational creatures’ free will” (p. 31, n. 79, citing Ramelli p. 113), and evil vanishing “according to its ontological non-subsistence” (nn. 83-84). Sytsma adds (p. 32) that, like Tzamalikos, Ramelli “does not state why this is so, only that it must be so”.
readings.side: reads the end of evil as the natural result of free choices, so restoration is universal and free

readings.scholar: Ilaria L. E. Ramelli
readings.work: Review of Cinzia Arruzza, Les mésaventures de la théodicée, Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2012.12.31
readings.position: Cites On First Principles 3.6.5 (a section not obtained here) for the sentence “Nihil enim omnipotenti impossibile est, nec insanabile est aliquid Factori suo” (nothing is impossible to the Almighty, nor is anything incurable by its Maker) and argues that the eventual apokatastasis rests “not on creatures’ lack of freedom, but on the omnipotence of the Logos”.
readings.side: reads the chapter as grounding restoration in God’s omnipotence, not in coercing freedom

passages.title: Where Rufinus and Justinian's Greek disagree: the Son as ‘image of God's goodness’ (On First Principles 1.2.13)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 1.2.13: Rufinus's Latin, and a Greek fragment preserved at the end of Justinian's Letter to Menas (543; Patrologia Graeca 86.1, Mansi 9)
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus 397-98; Justinian 543
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus) and Greek (Justinian's quotation, as Migne prints it)
passages.original: RUFINUS: (1.2.13) Superest quid sit imago bonitatis ejus inquirere: in quo eadem, ut opinor, intelligi convenit quae superius de imagine ea quae per speculum deformatur, expressimus. [Greek fragment inserted here by Migne, see below] Principalis namque bonitas sine dubio, ex qua Filius natus; qui per omnia imago est Patris, procul dubio etiam boni[…] talis ejus convenienter imago dicetur. Non enim alia aliqua secunda bonitas exsistit in Filio praeter eam quae est in Patre. Unde et recte ipse Salvator in Evangelio dicit quoniam « nemo bonus nisi unus Deus Pater »; quo scilicet per hoc intelligatur Filius non esse alterius bonitatis, sed illius solius quae in Patre est; cujus, recte imago appellatur, quia neque aliunde est, nisi ex ipsa principali bonitate; ne altera bonitas quam ea quae in Patre est, videatur in Filio. Neque aliqua dissimilitudo aut distantia bonitatis in Filio est. || JUSTINIAN (Greek, as printed in PG 11, col. 143-144, note 56): Οὗτω τοίνυν ἡγοῦμαι· καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος καλῶς ἂν λεχθήσεσθαι ὅτι εἰκὼν ἀγαθότητος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν· καὶ τάχα καὶ Υἱὸς ἀγαθός, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὡς ἁπλῶς ἀγαθός. Καὶ ὥσπερ εἰκὼν ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου, καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο Θεός, ἀλλ’ οὐ περὶ οὗ λέγει αὐτὸς ὁ Χριστός· ‘ἵνα γινώσκωσί σε τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεόν’, οὕτως εἰκὼν ἀγαθότητος, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὡς ὁ Πατὴρ ἀπαραλλάκτως ἀγαθός.
passages.edition: Latin: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), 1.2.13, page not confirmed. Greek: Justinian, Letter to Menas, Mansi 9 and PG 86.1 (neither opened); Koetschau prints it among his Greek fragments. Editions compared by Martens: Koetschau (1913); H. Gorgemanns and H. Karpp, Origenes: Vier Bucher von den Prinzipien (Darmstadt, 1976); Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978); Behr, OECT (2017).
passages.checked_against: Both texts as printed in Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 143-144 and note 56 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, second batch, page 076), checked against the OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11 scans (hvd page 077, mdp 085, njp 081). The three-column page runs Latin and Greek together, so the Latin is quoted only where contiguous, with […] at the one gap I could not close. Second pass: the Greek does not break off where the draft said; its remaining words are at the head of the next column of the same OCR page. Greek OCR slips fixed: ἡγομαι to ἡγοῦμαι, ν to ἂν, εκὼν to εἰκὼν (the njp scan also reads ἡγοῦμαι and ἂν), and ἀπλῶς (smooth breathing in the scan) to ἁπλῶς. The Greek was NOT checked against Justinian's letter itself.
passages.english: RUFINUS: (1.2.13) It remains to ask what the image of his goodness is; in this, I think, the same must be understood as we set out above about the image formed in a mirror. For the primary goodness is, without doubt, that from which the Son is born, who in everything is the image of the Father, and so without doubt also [… uncertain join] he will fittingly be called the image of such goodness of his. For no second goodness of any other kind exists in the Son besides the one that is in the Father. Hence the Saviour himself rightly says in the Gospel, ‘None is good but one, God the Father’, so that by this it may be understood that the Son is not of another goodness, but of that one goodness alone which is in the Father, whose image he is rightly called, because he is from nowhere else than from the primary goodness itself, lest another goodness than the one that is in the Father may seem to be in the Son. There is no unlikeness or distance of goodness in the Son. || JUSTINIAN’S GREEK: So, then, I think that of the Saviour too it would rightly be said that he is an image of God’s goodness, but not goodness itself; and perhaps also that the Son is good, but not good without qualification. And just as he is the image of the invisible God, and in that respect God, but not the one of whom Christ himself says, ‘That they may know you, the only true God’, so he is the image of goodness, but not, as the Father is, good without any variation.
passages.english_source: Own translation of the Latin and of the whole Greek sentence. Martens's gloss of the end of the first Greek sentence, ‘not purely and simply good’, agrees with ἁπλῶς in the scan (page of Martens's gloss not confirmed). ἀπαραλλάκτως is rendered ‘without any variation’ (Delarue’s own Latin version has ‘sine ulla differentia’). Standard translations: Butterworth (1936), Behr (2017), neither opened. Contested rendering: ‘ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν’ (not goodness itself) against Rufinus's ‘no other goodness’: the first makes the Son's goodness derived and lesser, the second says it is the Father's goodness.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the clearest small case of the editions problem, and Peter Martens uses it for that purpose. If the Greek is Origen's, Rufinus has made the Son's goodness equal to the Father's; if Rufinus is right, Justinian's quotation is doctored or taken out of context. It is not about universal salvation itself, but every dispute over what Origen taught on the end turns on the same prior question: trust Rufinus's Latin, or the hostile Greek? The same fork appears at 3.6.3 (the Greek fragment on God ‘all in all’ above).
passages.textual_notes: Delarue (note 56 in PG 11) printed the Greek in square brackets inside Rufinus's Latin and wrote that Justinian gives it at the end of his Letter to Menas, that he thinks it stood in the Greek text at this place, and that ‘it is clear how unreliable the faith of Rufinus is, who omitted it and substituted other things’ (own translation of ‘liquet quam fluxa sit fides Rufini qui ea omiserit et alia substituerit’). He adds a Latin version of the Greek ending ‘fortasse etiam Filium bonum, sed non simpliciter bonum … ita bonitatis imago, non tamen ut Pater, sine ulla differentia bonus’. The Greek as Migne prints it has ‘καλῶς ἂν λεχθήσεσθαι’, an irregular construction (ἄν with a future infinitive) that may be a corruption; I kept it. Jerome had already complained (Letter to Avitus, quoted in Delarue’s note 56) that Origen here ‘calls God the Father omnipotent, good and of perfect goodness; the Son not good, but a breath and an image of goodness, so that he is not called absolutely good, but with an addition, ’the good shepherd’’. Note 57 gives the manuscript reading of Rufinus: ‘ne altera bonitas quam ea quae in Patre est, videatur in Filio’ (earlier editions: ‘exsistit in Filium praeter eam quae est a Patre’). Martens reports (p. 321, in his text, not in n. 43) that Koetschau supports the Greek by a parallel at Commentary on Matthew 15.10, where Origen says the predicate ‘good’ is properly attributed only to God the Father. Koetschau's own page and line not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader) and Charles Delarue (editor)
readings.work: Jerome, Letter to Avitus (Letter 124), as quoted in Delarue's note 56, PG 11 cols. 143-144; Delarue's edition of Origen (1733-59) as reprinted in PG 11
readings.position: Both take the Greek in Justinian's letter as what Origen wrote and Rufinus as having left it out. Delarue says so in as many words (‘how unreliable the faith of Rufinus is’); Jerome complains that Origen made the Son a mere image of goodness.
readings.side: trusts the hostile Greek and Jerome against Rufinus

readings.scholar: Paul Koetschau and Hermann Görgemanns-Heinrich Karpp (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Martens, ‘The Modern Editions of Peri Archon’, Journal of Early Christian Studies 28.2 (2020), pp. 303-331, esp. pp. 313, 315, 317, 321 and n. 43
readings.position: Martens puts them, with Delarue, Rius-Camps and Fernández, in a group that prints a ‘mosaicked’ text (pp. 313, 315), and writes that “Each of the editors in group two regards Justinian’s fragment as genuine and Rufinus’s corresponding translation as corrupt” (p. 321). Of Koetschau he says that he “distinguishes himself … by interrupting the progression of Rufinus’s translation so frequently” (p. 317).
readings.side: trusts the Greek fragment and builds the Latin text around it

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel and Manlio Simonetti (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Martens, JECS 28.2 (2020), pp. 313-315, 321 n. 43; Crouzel’s commentary volume to SC 252-253 (1978)
readings.position: Martens places their edition in the group that “primarily prints Rufinus’s translation” (p. 313). On this passage he writes in n. 43 (p. 321) that “even Crouzel, in his lengthy note, concedes that Justinian’s report is ‘perhaps authentic’”.
readings.side: prints Rufinus; allows the Greek may be authentic

readings.scholar: John Behr (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Origen: On First Principles, Oxford Early Christian Texts (OUP, 2017); Martens, JECS 28.2 (2020), p. 314
readings.position: Martens writes that Behr, like Crouzel and Simonetti, “presents a continuous and complete text of Rufinus’s Latin translation” and prints parallel sources at the foot of the relevant pages. Martens’s lines that I could read do not say what Behr makes of 1.2.13 itself.
readings.side: prints Rufinus as the continuous text, with other witnesses beside it

readings.scholar: G. W. Butterworth, as characterised by John Cavadini and Daniel Heide
readings.work: Cavadini, Foreword to Origen: On First Principles (Christian Classics/Ave Maria Press, 2013 reprint of Butterworth), pp. vii-viii; Heide, Arc 44 (2016), pp. 57, 59-60 and n. 46
readings.position: Cavadini writes that Koetschau’s presentation “was predicated on a hermeneutic of thoroughgoing suspicion regarding Rufinus’s translation”, that Butterworth “fully adopted, and even extended” it, “divided the page between” Latin and Greek columns, and used sources “as hostile as the anathemata of Justinian” (pp. vii-viii). Heide agrees, calling Butterworth’s confidence that Jerome does not exaggerate “mindboggling” (p. 60) and Crouzel and Simonetti “an important corrective to Koetschau” (p. 57). Neither speaks of 1.2.13 specifically, and I did not open Butterworth.
readings.side: critics of the Koetschau-Butterworth method, who trust Rufinus more

passages.title: Why the full teaching on punishment is not for the many (Against Celsus 6.26)
passages.original: Ὅσα δ᾿ εἰς τὸν τόπον λεχθείη ἂν, οὔτε πᾶσιν οὔτε τοῦ παρόντος καιροῦ ἐστι διηγήσασθαι· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἀκίνδυνον τὴν τῶν τοιούτων σαφήνειαν πιστεῦσαι γραφῇ. ἅτε τῶν πολλῶν οὐ χρῃζόντων πλείονος διδασκαλίας παρὰ τὴν περὶ τῆς κατὰ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων κολάσεως. εἰς γὰρ τὰ ὑπερέκεινα αὐτῆς οὐ χρήσιμον ἀναβαίνειν διὰ τοὺς μόγις φόβῳ τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως κἂν συστέλλοντας ἐπὶ ποσὸν τῆς κακίας καὶ τῶν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἁμαρτανομένων χύσιν.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke vol. 2 (= Buch V-VIII gegen Kelsos, GCS 3, Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1899), p. 96: the Perseus transcription marks the start of p. 96 just before chapter 26 and no later page break falls before these lines. Line numbers not given. Modern translation: H. Chadwick, Contra Celsum (Cambridge, 1953), not opened. Public-domain English: ANF 4 (Crombie), seen only in short phrases (below).
passages.checked_against: Perseus Digital Library TEI transcription of Koetschau (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg001.perseus-grc1), which carries Koetschau's page numbers. One obvious typing slip fixed: πολῶν to πολλῶν. Second pass: compared letter for letter, with accents, against that file, and against a second text of the same chapter on bkv.unifr.ch (edition not named on the page), which has the same wording (it prints ἄν for ἂν in the first sentence) and the same πολλῶν. Both are electronic transcriptions, not the printed page.
passages.english: As for what might be said on this subject, it is neither for everyone nor for the present occasion to set it out; and it is not free of danger to entrust the plain statement of such matters to writing, since the many need no more teaching than the one about the punishment of sinners. To go beyond it is not useful, because of those who, barely, through fear of eternal punishment, hold back to some extent the outpouring of evil and of the sins that come from it.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Compare ANF 4 (Crombie, public domain), whose English as shown on bkv.unifr.ch (translator not named there) has ‘nor to be uttered on the present occasion’, ‘not unattended with danger to commit to writing’ and ‘fear of eternal punishment’. Contested rendering: ‘αἰωνίου κολάσεως’ (eternal punishment; or age-long, lasting for an age, the meaning argued by Ramelli and Konstan for aionios, see the Romans 6.5 entry). Note that Origen himself uses the word here in the phrase the many fear, and does not say whether he thinks it is the right word. ‘τὸν τόπον’ (this subject, this place): the lines before it speak of purification by fire in Jerusalem, so the subject is the fire of punishment.
passages.why_it_matters: This is a passage cited (by Batiffol and by Heide, among those read here) for the claim that Origen held a fuller doctrine than he taught the simple. He says the plain account of punishment is enough for the many and that going beyond it would not help those who are held back from evil by fear of an ‘eternal’ punishment. He does not say what lies beyond it, and he does not call the doctrine of eternal punishment false.
passages.textual_notes: The extract begins mid-argument; the previous sentence in 6.26 (not quoted) speaks of punishments ‘in connection with Jerusalem’, of souls being melted down, and of Zechariah's ‘talent of lead’. No variant of consequence is recorded in the transcription. Chapter division is Koetschau's.

readings.scholar: Pierre Batiffol
readings.work: ‘Apocatastasis’, Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (1907); copy read on catholic.com
readings.position: Says Origen “does not seem to have regarded the doctrine of the apokatastasis as one meant to be preached to all”, citing Against Celsus VI, 26. Elsewhere in the article he writes that Origen “seems at times reluctant to decide” on the eternity of punishment, and that “as a rule, Origen teaches the apokatastasis”; he cites On First Principles 1.6.3 (Origen “does not venture to assert” that all evil angels will return) on the other side, relying on Tixeront.
readings.side: reads Origen as teaching apokatastasis as a rule, but cautiously and not publicly

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), p. 197 n. 13
readings.position: Suggests that the devil’s ultimate fate (like the non-eternity of hell) “perhaps belongs” among the things of which Origen says “It is not right to explain to everybody all that might be said on this subject” (his English for 6.26). He adds that “the logic of Origen’s ontology seems to require the conversion and ultimate restoration of the devil”.
readings.side: reads the reticence as probably hiding a universalist conclusion

readings.scholar: Tom Greggs (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 27 and n. 81 (Greggs, p. 315; work not named in the part I could read, probably Greggs’s article on Origen in the International Journal of Systematic Theology 8.3, 2006, which I have not opened)
readings.position: Hannen cites Greggs for the claim that “Origen clearly took a different stance on universalism dependent on the genre of his work”. The point about audience is Hannen’s own (p. 22).
readings.side: reads Origen’s wording as adjusted to genre, not as inconsistency

passages.title: The Word will master every rational soul, and evil will be abolished (Against Celsus 8.72)
passages.original: ἡμεῖς δὲ τῆς λογικῆς φύσεώς φαμεν ὅλης κρατῆσαί ποτε τὸν λόγον καὶ μεταποιῆσαι πᾶσαν ψυχὴν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελειότητα, ἐπὰν [289] ἕκαστος ψιλῇ χρησάμενος τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ἕληται ἃ βούλεται καὶ γένηται ἐν οἷς εἵλατο· καὶ φαμεν ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν εἰκὸς, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ⟨ἐν⟩ τοῖς σώμασι νοσημάτων καὶ τραυμάτων τινὰ τῶν συμβαινόντων ἰσχυρότερα εἶναι πάσης ἰατρικῆς τέχνης, οὕτως ἐπὶ τῶν ψυχῶν εἶναί τι τῶν ἀπὸ κακίας ἀδύνατον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι λογικοῦ καὶ θεοῦ θεραπευθῆναι. πάντων γὰρ τῶν ἐν ψυχῇ κακῶν δυνατώτερος ὢν ὁ λόγος καὶ ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ θεραπεία προσάγει κατὰ βούλησιν θεοῦ ἑκάστῳ αὐτὴν, καὶ τὸ τέλος τῶν πραγμάτων ἀναιρεθῆναί ἐστι τὴν κακίαν· πότερον δὲ ὥστε μηδαμῇ μηδαμῶς ἔτι αὐτὴν ἐπιτραπῆναι δύνασθαι ἢ μὴ, οὐ τοῦ παρόντος ἐστὶ λόγου διδάξαι.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke 2, GCS 3 (Leipzig, 1899), pp. 288-289 (the bracketed [289] marks Koetschau's page break; ⟨ἐν⟩ is an editorial supplement (the digital text tags it as an addition and prints it in round brackets; I could not confirm from the printed page that it is Koetschau's own)). Chadwick (1953) and ANF 4 not opened.
passages.checked_against: Perseus TEI transcription of Koetschau (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg001.perseus-grc1) with his page numbers. Two stray page markers from the digital file (not Koetschau's) were removed, one of which fell in the middle of the word αὐτήν. The transcription is electronic, not the printed page. Second pass (fact-check): compared letter for letter, with accents, against that file; the only differences are the two page markers removed, the angle brackets I use for the supplement ⟨ἐν⟩ (the file has it as an <add> in round brackets), and the [289] I kept to show his page break.
passages.english: But we say that the Word will one day master the whole rational nature and remake every soul into his own perfection, when each, using only his own freedom, chooses what he wishes and becomes what he has chosen. And we say that, as with diseases and wounds of bodies some are stronger than every medical art, it is not likely that among souls anything arising from evil is incurable by the Word, who is over all, and by God. For the Word, being more powerful than all the evils in the soul, and the healing that is in him, brings it to each according to God's will; and the end of things is that evil is abolished. Whether so that it can in no way ever again be allowed [to arise], or not, is not for the present discussion to teach.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Compare ANF 4 (Crombie, public domain; as shown on bkv.unifr.ch, translator not named there): ‘The consummation of all things is the destruction of evil’ and ‘whether it shall be so destroyed that it can never anywhere arise again, it is beyond our present purpose to say’. Standard comparisons: Chadwick (1953); ANF 4 (public domain, Crombie); neither opened. Contested renderings: ‘κρατῆσαι’ (master, prevail over, gain control of); ‘μεταποιῆσαι’ (remake or transform); ‘ἀναιρεθῆναι τὴν κακίαν’ (that evil be abolished, taken away, destroyed); ‘ἐπιτραπῆναι’ in the last clause (be allowed, be given leave, be turned over: the sentence leaves open whether evil could ever be readmitted).
passages.why_it_matters: This is a direct statement, in a late work (c. 248, by the date above), that the aim of the Word's healing is to abolish evil in every rational soul. He says it as what ‘we’ say, not as a guess. Then he refuses to decide, in this discussion, whether evil could ever return. Readers divide over how much weight the first half carries and how much the refusal carries.
passages.textual_notes: There is no ‘perhaps’ (τάχα) in these lines of Koetschau's Greek, although the passage is sometimes quoted as if there were. The hedge is the closing sentence, which explicitly sets aside the question whether evil can be so abolished that it can never again be admitted. The next sentences (not quoted) bring in Zephaniah 3:7-11 as prophetic support. Against Celsus survives in Greek in the Tura papyrus for books 1-2 and in the manuscript tradition for the rest, so Rufinus's problem does not arise here. The Greek reads λογικοῦ (‘rational’) in “ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι λογικοῦ καὶ θεοῦ”, in both texts I compared; I translate it, as translators do, as the Word (λόγου). The last clause (ἐπιτραπῆναι δύνασθαι) is awkward Greek and is rendered differently by different translators. The page markers v.2.p.288 and p.289 in the digital text put this chapter on pp. 288-289 of Koetschau's volume. A second text of the chapter (bkv.unifr.ch) gives the same Greek for the three clauses I compared.

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 27 and nn. 72-74
readings.position: Cites 8.72 (n. 72) for the claim that the end of the Word’s treatment is the abolition of evil, and so reads the passage as pointing to universal restoration. He sets beside it Contra Celsum 3.16 and 3.31 (nn. 73-74, p. 27), passages that seem to point to separation after death.
readings.side: reads 8.72 as a statement of universal restoration

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, p. 27 and n. 82 (Crouzel, pp. 257-266)
readings.position: Hannen cites Crouzel for “The best we can ascertain is that Origen hoped for universal salvation”. This is Crouzel’s general position, not a comment on 8.72 by number.
readings.side: reads Origen as hoping for, not asserting, universal salvation

readings.scholar: Ronald E. Heine (as cited by Chris Hannen; first name and work supplied from memory, not confirmed from Hannen) and Ilaria Ramelli
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2, pp. 27-28 and nn. 85-86 (Heine, p. 256; Ramelli, p. 316)
readings.position: Hannen quotes Heine as calling it “a defendable, but not an unquestionable, conclusion” that Origen was rethinking universal restoration at Caesarea, and himself concludes there was no “major recant or u-turn” (p. 28). He cites Ramelli (n. 86) on the other side. Against Celsus is a late work (c. 248), so this bears on how to read 8.72.
readings.side: Heine: late rethinking is defensible; Hannen and Ramelli: continuity

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Steven Nemes)
readings.work: Nemes, review of Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis, Journal of Analytic Theology 3 (May 2015), pp. 228-229 (page range inferred from running heads), citing Ramelli (Brill, 2013), pp. 193, 208
readings.position: Nemes quotes “No being is incurable for the Christ-Logos” (citing Ramelli p. 193; he does not make clear whether the words are Ramelli’s or Origen’s) and “Apokatastasis is professed by Origen in all of his works” (citing p. 208). Nemes does not link either to 8.72; they match its argument and are placed here for that reason.
readings.side: reads Origen as consistently teaching that the Logos can heal every being

readings.scholar: Ilaria L. E. Ramelli
readings.work: Review of Cinzia Arruzza, Les mésaventures de la théodicée, Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2012.12.31
readings.position: Cites Contra Celsum 8.72 together with On First Principles 3.6.5 to argue that God’s omnipotence guarantees the cure of even ‘incurable’ souls, and says the eventual apokatastasis rests “not on creatures’ lack of freedom, but on the omnipotence of the Logos”.
readings.side: reads 8.72 as grounding the end of evil in the Logos’s power, not in loss of freedom

passages.title: ‘You deceived me, Lord’: the physician, the father and the hidden mystery (Homilies on Jeremiah 20.3-4)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Homilies on Jeremiah, Homily 20, sections 3-4 (on Jeremiah 20:7)
passages.original: (20.3, p. 181) τὸ κατὰ τὸν τόπον μυστήριον κεκρύφθαι δεῖ, ἵνα μὴ ἐκκακήσῃ ὁ πολύς, ἵνα μὴ μαθὼν τὰ πράγματα προσδοκήσῃ τὴν ἔξοδον οὐχ ὡς ἀνάπαυσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς κόλασιν. (20.3, p. 182) ἄλλη γὰρ ἡ ἀπάτη ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἄλλη ἡ ἀπάτη ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως. (20.4, p. 183) πόσοι δὲ νομιζόμενοι σοφοί, εὑρόντες τὸ περὶ κολάσεως ἀληθὲς καὶ διελθόντες δῆθεν τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης, ἐν χείρονι γεγόνασι βίῳ; ἐλυσιτέλει αὐτοὺς φρονεῖν, ὡς ἐφρόνουν πρότερον περὶ τοῦ ‘ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτήσει’ καὶ ὅτι ‘τὸ πῦρ αὐτῶν οὐ σβεσθήσεται’
passages.edition: E. Klostermann, Origenes Werke 3: Jeremiahomilien, Klageliederkommentar, Erklarung der Samuelbucher, GCS 6 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1901), Homily 20.3-4, pp. 179-184 (the quoted lines fall on pp. 181, 182 and 183 by the page markers in the digital file). A second edition by P. Nautin appeared in 1983, and P. Nautin and P. Husson edited the Greek with French translation in SC 232 and 238 (1976-77; I believe Homily 20 is in SC 238); I did not check either. A German edition and translation by A. Fürst and H. E. Lona is mentioned by Somos (2025, p. 95); not checked. English: J. C. Smith, Fathers of the Church 97 (1998), not opened.
passages.checked_against: TEI transcription of Klostermann (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg021.opp-grc1), which keeps Klostermann's page numbers and his editorial marks. One obvious typing slip fixed: πρότρον to πρότερον. Electronic transcription, not the printed page. Second pass: compared letter for letter, with accents, against that file; the only differences are the πρότερον fix and the quotation marks. The page numbers 181, 182 and 183 agree with the page markers in the XML. No second text of the Greek was found.
passages.english: (20.3) The mystery in this passage has to be kept hidden, so that the many may not lose heart, so that, learning how things are, they may not expect their departure as a rest but as a punishment. (20.3) For the deception from God is one thing, the deception from the serpent another. (20.4) How many who are thought wise, having found the truth about punishment and gone through, as they suppose, the business of the deception, have fallen into a worse way of life? It would have profited them to go on thinking as they used to think about ‘their worm shall not die’ and ‘their fire shall not be quenched’.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Contested renderings: ‘ἀπάτη’ and the verb of Jeremiah 20:7 (the Septuagint's ἠπάτησάς με: deceived, tricked; the Hebrew verb is commonly rendered ‘enticed’ or ‘persuaded’, which fits Origen's argument that the deception is for the person's good); ‘δῆθεν’ (supposedly, as they think); ‘τὸ περὶ κολάσεως ἀληθές’ (the truth about punishment: the lines quoted do not say what it is; see the textual notes for the example just before them).
passages.why_it_matters: With Against Celsus 6.26 this is where Origen most openly says that what the many are told about punishment may differ from what the wise are told. The disputed point is what the ‘truth about punishment’ is. Read closely, 20.3 says the hidden thing is that the baptised too must pass through punishment (the preceding lines say every sinner must be punished, and that his own ‘wood’ must be burned in him), not that all will be saved; 20.4 says some who found the truth took it for permission and did worse. The lines quoted do not themselves say what the truth is. The example given just before them (see the textual notes) suggests it is milder than the ‘eternal’ punishment the many fear, in the case of the twice-married, but the homily does not say that punishment ends for all.
passages.textual_notes: Klostermann's text has a gap in 20.3 (‘. . .’) after ‘καὶ τὸν σοφώτατον’, where the manuscript is defective or the editor sees a lacuna; the sentence just before the quoted lines is broken for the same reason. Another clause early in 20.3 reads ‘οὖν ἄλλως δυνάμενον’ in the transcription, which may be a slip for ‘οὐκ ἄλλως’; it is not quoted. The Greek homilies were preserved in a few manuscripts. Whether Jerome's Latin translation of fourteen homilies has a counterpart for Homily 20 was not checked. Context from the same section, in the lines just before the quotation of 20.4: Origen gives an example of a useful deception. It is more profitable for a woman married once to think that the twice-married woman is ‘punished and handed over to eternal [αἰωνίῳ] punishment’ (κολάζεσθαι καὶ αἰωνίῳ κολάσει παραδίδοσθαι) so that she stays chaste, than to know the truth and marry again; and the truth, he says, is ‘that the twice-married woman too has a share in some salvation, though not in so great a blessedness’ (μετέχει μὲν σωτηρίας τινὸς καὶ ἡ δίγαμος, οὐ μὴν τοσαύτης μακαριότητος). So in this homily the ‘deception’ includes at least a belief in ‘eternal’ punishment for some, and the ‘truth’ is milder; whether Origen extends that to all sinners is not said in the lines quoted. (My own reading of the Greek, own translation; not a scholar's.)

readings.scholar: Róbert Somos
readings.work: Introduction to his Hungarian translation, ‘Órigenész: Huszadik homília Jeremiás könyvéhez’, Vállástudományi szemle 2025/1, pp. 93-110, at p. 94
readings.position: Says Origen “does not speak of a lie in the strict sense” (“nem szoros értelemben vett hazugságról beszél”) but of leaving certain things unsaid, and that God acts like a physician or a father who deceives for the patient’s or child’s good. The introduction does not discuss the marriage example in 20.4.
readings.side: reads the ‘deception’ as concealment for the hearer’s good, not lying

passages.title: Love never fails: can restored beings fall again? (Commentary on Romans 5.10)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans 5.10 (on Romans 6:9-10), Rufinus's abridged Latin translation; Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1053-1054
passages.date: Origen's Greek c. 244 (dating uncertain); Rufinus's Latin c. 405-407
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's abridged translation; no Greek survives for this part)
passages.original: … potest fieri ut in quocunque statu fuerit anima, et in quacunque perfectione virtutum, quoniam virtus mutabilis est, lapsum possit incurrere … Haec ergo et his similia proponentes, easdem etiam in futuris saeculis dispensationes a Christo repetendas esse arbitrantur. Sed ad haec nos breviter prout possumus respondebimus. Manere quidem naturae rationabili semper liberum arbitrium non negamus; sed tantam esse vim crucis Christi, et mortis hujus, quam in saeculorum fine suscepit, asserimus, quae ad sanitatem et remedium non solum praesentis et futuri, sed etiam praeteritorum saeculorum, et non solum humano huic nostro ordini, sed etiam caelestibus virtutibus ordinibusque sufficiat. … Quid autem sit quod in futuris saeculis teneat arbitrii libertatem, ne rursum corruat in peccatum, brevi nos sermone Apostolus docet, dicens: ‘Charitas nunquam cadit.’ Idcirco enim et fide et spe major charitas dicitur, quia sola erit per quam delinqui ultra non poterit. … Et ideo merito charitas quae sola omnium major est, omnem creaturam continebit a lapsu. Tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus.
passages.edition: C. P. Hammond Bammel, Der Romerbrief-Kommentar des Origenes: kritische Ausgabe der Ubersetzung Rufins, Vetus Latina: Aus der Geschichte der lateinischen Bibel 16, 33, 34 (Freiburg: Herder, 1990, 1997, 1998); Books 4-6 should be in the second volume, 33 (1997), and Books 7-10 in 34 (1998); I recall this from the series list and did not confirm it; not opened, page not confirmed. English: T. P. Scheck, Origen: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Fathers of the Church 103 (2001), where a web post puts Book 5.10 at p. 376; not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Hammond Bammel. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1053-1054 (Delarue's text), from the OCR page transcription OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-14 (nyp.33433081862280_ocr, page 538). The page has two columns read line by line; the quoted sentences were put back in order and the lemma lines of the right-hand column (the Romans text being commented on) left out. ‘Charitas nunquam cadit’ is from 1 Corinthians 13:8. Spelling and ligatures normalised (c/ch left as printed). The page header says Book 5 (‘LIB. V’); the chapter number 5.10 is the survey's own reference to the passage, not something the scan shows. Second pass: the Latin was re-read against the same page; every word of it is there, in the order the draft gives, and Delarue's notes 51 and 53 read as described.
passages.english: … it can happen that in whatever state the soul has been, and in whatever perfection of virtues, since virtue can change, it may incur a fall … [Those] who put forward these and similar arguments think that the same dispensations must be repeated by Christ in future ages. But to these we shall reply briefly, as well as we can. We do not deny that free choice remains with rational nature always; but we declare that the power of Christ's cross, and of this death which he took upon himself at the end of the ages, is enough for the healing and remedy not only of the present and the future, but also of the past ages, and not only of this human order of ours but also of the heavenly powers and orders. … What it is that preserves freedom of choice in the ages to come, so that it does not fall back into sin, the Apostle teaches us in a few words, saying: ‘Love never falls.’ For that is why love is called greater than faith and hope: because it alone will be the means by which there can be no more sinning. … And so, rightly, love, which alone is greater than all, will keep the whole creation from falling. Then God will be all in all.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard English: Scheck (FC 103, 2001), not opened. Contested renderings: ‘saeculum’ (age, world or epoch); ‘charitas’ (love or charity); ‘creaturam continebit a lapsu’ (will hold the whole creation back from falling); ‘liberum arbitrium’ (free choice or free will).
passages.why_it_matters: This is Origen's answer, as Rufinus gives it, to the objection that a creature with free choice could fall again even after being restored, so that the saving work would have to be repeated in each future age. Jerome claimed Origen's system ended in endless cycles of rise and fall (Letter 124); this passage says the opposite, that love will secure the creation, which is where it can be set against Jerome (this survey's own observation, not a scholar's). It also does not say that every being is already restored.
passages.textual_notes: Rufinus says in his preface that he shortened the Commentary on Romans, which ran to fifteen books in Greek, to ten (the usual account; I did not check who first gives the number; Sytsma cites the preface only for the abridgment). The small Greek papyrus finds from Tura cover only Romans 3:5-5:7 in this commentary (Scherer 1957, usual reference, unchecked), so there is no Greek control at 5.10. The PG apparatus: note 51, ‘nec’ would suit the sense better than ‘ne rursum corruat’, but all manuscripts and editions read ‘ne’; note 53, the final clause ‘Tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus’ is preceded in earlier editions and one manuscript by different wording (‘maxima est … tunc cum erit Deus’ and ‘mater est … cum erit Deus’). The lemma it comments on is Romans 6:10 (‘the life he lives, he lives to God’).

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as quoted by Aidan Kimel)
readings.work: Kimel, ‘An Open Letter to Dr Cyril Jenkins’ (2024), n. 10, citing Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Brill, 2013), p. 152 (the book is cited at pp. 137-215 for her defence of Origen’s universalism)
readings.position: Kimel quotes, in n. 10, a passage of the Commentary on Romans saying the power of Christ’s cross “is so great as to be enough to set right and save, not only the present and the future aeon, but also all the past ones”. He gives no section number; I matched it to 5.10 myself. He uses it, with Ramelli, for the claim that “Despite his disclaimer, Origen really does believe that all will be saved.”
readings.side: reads the passage as evidence that Origen really believed in universal salvation despite his disclaimer

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), p. 24 and n. 55, citing Crouzel, Origen (1985; English translation 1989), pp. 264-65
readings.position: In a block quotation Sytsma gives Crouzel’s view that “Certainty about a universal apocatastasis would be in contradiction to the authenticity of the free will” and that it “could only be a great hope”. This states the problem 5.10 is written to answer, but the report does not discuss 5.10 itself.
readings.side: holds that freedom rules out certainty of universal salvation

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 124 to Avitus, 124.3.6 (Hilberg, CSEL 56, p. 99), Latin as recorded in this survey’s c400 file
readings.position: Charges that Origen’s system means rational creatures change places “not once and suddenly but repeatedly”: we shall be angels and, if we act carelessly, demons; and demons, if they lay hold of virtue, will reach angelic dignity. (The survey’s own observation, not Jerome’s: if Rufinus’s Romans commentary is Origen’s own, 5.10 answers that charge.)
readings.side: ancient hostile reader: reads Origen’s system as allowing endless falls

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, dissertation, p. 31 and n. 79, citing Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (2013), p. 113
readings.position: Sytsma quotes Ramelli: “Providence does not force rational creatures’ free will”, and that once souls know the Good “all will voluntarily adhere to the Good” (p. 31). He adds (p. 32) that she “does not state why this is so, only that it must be so”. Again the report is about the problem, not 5.10.
readings.side: holds that providence and freedom agree, so restoration is secure and free

passages.title: What ‘eternal’ means: a lifetime, an age, or without end (Commentary on Romans 6.5)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans 6.5 (on Romans 6:22-23), Rufinus's abridged Latin translation; Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1067-1068
passages.date: Origen's Greek c. 244 (dating uncertain); Rufinus's Latin c. 405-407
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's abridged translation; Greek for this passage not known to survive; the catena and papyrus fragments of the commentary were not checked)
passages.original: … et erit tibi servus in aeternum. Aeternum hic sine dubio tempus vitae hominis posuit. Et iterum in Ecclesiaste dicitur: ‘Generatio vadit, et generatio venit, terra autem in aeternum stat’: hic aeternum praesentis saeculi tempus ostendit. Ubi vero dicit ‘vitam aeternam,’ ad illud aspiciendum est quod ipse Salvator dixit: ‘Haec est autem vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum …’ … Sicut ergo semper cum Domino esse, finem non habet, ita et vita aeterna nullum finem habere credenda est. … Ego non puto etiam hoc vacuum esse, quod ad vitam aeternam addidit ‘in Christo [Jesu] Domino nostro’; sed quia fortassis sciri voluit aliud esse vitam aeternam solum, et aliud vitam aeternam in Christo Jesu. Et illi enim qui surgent in confusionem et opprobrium sempiternum, habebunt quidem vitam aeternam, non tamen in Christo Jesu, sed in confusione et opprobrio aeterno; justi vero qui surgent in vitam aeternam in Christo Jesu habebunt vitam aeternam.
passages.edition: C. P. Hammond Bammel, Der Römerbriefkommentar des Origenes: kritische Ausgabe der Übersetzung Rufins, Vetus Latina: Aus der Geschichte der lateinischen Bibel 16 (Books 1-3, 1990), 33 (Books 4-6, 1997) and 34 (Books 7-10, 1998) (Freiburg: Herder). Book 6 should be in volume 33; I recall the volume numbers from the series list and did not open any of them. Page not confirmed. English: T. P. Scheck, Origen: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Books 6-10, Fathers of the Church 104 (Catholic University of America Press, 2002); not opened. Heide (Dionysius 33, n. 27) cites a sentence of the Romans commentary on ‘eternity’ as ‘Comm. Romans VI.5.9’; I could not tell whether that sentence lies in the lines printed here, or whether ‘.9’ is Scheck's or Hammond Bammel's section number.
passages.checked_against: NOT Hammond Bammel. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1067-1068 (Delarue's text), from the OCR page transcription OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-14 (nyp.33433081862280_ocr, page 545; the page's running number is garbled in the scan and reads like ‘1067’). The scan reads the two columns line by line, so the quoted sentences were put back in order. Second pass (fact-check): every sentence quoted was found again on that page, in the order given here. The sentence the draft left out (‘Et illi enim qui surgent …’) is on the page, reads clearly apart from the garbled ‘Jesu’ and a stray ‘576’ in the line, and is now included. Three places are restored by sense, not read: ‘Haec est’ in the John 17:3 quotation (garbled in the scan), ‘praesentis’ (garbled), and ‘Jesu’ in ‘non tamen in Christo Jesu’ (the scan has a garbled token where ‘Jesu’ is expected, as it does in both quotations of Romans 6:23 on the same page). In ‘quod ad vitam aeternam addidit in Christo Domino nostro’ the scan has no ‘Jesu’ at all, so it is bracketed above. The chapter number 6.5 is the survey's own reference to the passage, not something the scan shows.
passages.english: … and he will be your servant for ever [aeternum]. Here ‘for ever’ undoubtedly stands for the time of a man's life. And again, in Ecclesiastes it is said: ‘A generation goes and a generation comes, but the earth stands for ever’; here ‘for ever’ shows the time of the present age.
