But where he says ‘eternal life’, we must look to what the Saviour himself said: ‘This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God …’ … As, therefore, being always with the Lord has no end, so eternal life too must be believed to have no end. … I do not think even this is empty, that to ‘eternal life’ he added ‘in Christ [Jesus] our Lord’; perhaps he wanted it known that eternal life alone is one thing, and eternal life in Christ Jesus another. For even those who rise ‘to shame [confusionem] and everlasting [sempiternum] reproach’ will indeed have eternal life, though not in Christ Jesus: they will have it in shame and eternal [aeterno] reproach; but the righteous, who rise to eternal life in Christ Jesus, will have eternal life.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard English: Scheck (FC 104, 2002), not opened. The key word is Latin ‘aeternum’, presumably rendering Greek aionios (the Greek is lost; aion: an age; aionios: of the age, age-long, or, in later usage, eternal). Contested renderings: ‘in aeternum’ (for ever, for an age, for a lifetime); ‘vita aeterna’ (eternal life, or life of the age to come).
passages.why_it_matters: Scholars who argue that Origen himself knew ‘eternal’ can mean a stretch of time point to the Romans commentary (Heide does, quoting a sentence of it). Here, in Rufinus's Latin, ‘in aeternum’ is said to mean a man's lifetime in one verse and the present age in another, while eternal life with the Lord is said to have no end. The sentence the draft left out adds that those who rise to shame will also have ‘eternal life’, though not ‘in Christ Jesus’, and that their reproach is ‘eternal’ too, so ‘aeternus’ is used of the lot of the lost as well as of the saved. The passage therefore supports more than one reading: that ‘eternal’ need not mean endless; that Origen holds the life of the saved to be endless; and that he applies the same word to both lots. How much weight it carries in the dispute over eternal punishment depends on whether the word may mean an age in one place and without end in another, and on how far Rufinus's Latin can be trusted to carry Origen's Greek.
passages.textual_notes: Rufinus's abridgment and the lack of Greek mean the Latin ‘aeternum’ and ‘aeternam’ could stand for aionios or for another Greek word. Heide (Dionysius 33, p. 202) quotes a sentence of this commentary as ‘In the Scriptures “eternity” (aeternitas = αἰών) is sometimes recorded …’, which reads aeternitas as the Latin for aion; I did not find the Latin of that sentence on the Migne page used here. Delarue's apparatus on the page: note 26 says the printed editions (‘Editi’) read ‘quorum fructus ne nominare dignum’ and, for the second quotation of Romans 6:23, give only ‘Gratia autem Dei in Christo, etc.’, leaving out ‘vita aeterna’; note 28 gives ‘surgunt’ for ‘surgent’ and, a little later, ‘habent’ for ‘habebunt’ in the sentence about the two kinds of rising (Delarue's ‘Alias’, meaning other readings; the centuries of those editions are not stated). The scan is garbled at several points (‘Haec est’, ‘praesentis’, and ‘Jesu’ in three places, once as ‘ἔθευ’); the garbled words are restored by sense, and the ‘Jesu’ the scan lacks altogether in the sentence about ‘in Christo Domino nostro’ is bracketed rather than supplied. In the sentence the draft omitted, the Latin uses ‘aeternam’ of the life of the lost, ‘sempiternum’ of their reproach in the first clause and ‘aeterno’ in the second.

readings.position: Heide gives Crouzel's French. Its sense: the essential reason why the expression ‘eternal fire’ (πῦρ αἰώνιον) does not seem to Origen to imply necessarily the eternity of punishment “as we understand it” is that the adjective αἰώνιος “conserve pour lui tout l'ambiguïté du mot dont il dérive αἰών”; in both Testaments, beside ‘eternity’ as endless duration, one finds the sense ‘age’ (a long period, in particular the duration of the present world, or of the world to come). Heide's transcription has a few typing slips. This is a general statement about Origen's use of αἰώνιος, not a comment on the Romans commentary or on this passage.

other_findings.claim: Peter Martens divides the modern editors of Peri Archon into two groups: one “primarily prints Rufinus's translation” (Merlin, Crouzel and Simonetti, Behr; pp. 313-315), the other “prints a mosaicked text” (Delarue, Koetschau, Görgemanns and Karpp, Rius-Camps, Fernández; p. 315). other_findings.claim: John Cavadini says Koetschau's presentation “was predicated on a hermeneutic of thoroughgoing suspicion regarding Rufinus's translation” and that Butterworth “fully adopted, and even extended” it (p. vii); Butterworth “translated the only complete attestation of the text remaining from antiquity”, which is Rufinus's Latin (p. vii). The foreword does not mention Behr's edition, and says that in this reprint, except where the Philocalia gives “a substantial, continuous attestation of the text”, “the text of Rufinus stands alone”, other Greek fragments being omitted, with the omissions noted and referred to Crouzel and Simonetti's Sources Chrétiennes edition (p. viii). other_findings.claim: Daniel Heide argues that Koetschau and Butterworth supplemented Rufinus's text with material “from sources as hostile as the anathemata of Justinian” (p. 57), and that Butterworth “tells us without reservation that Koetschau inserted anathemas II to VI directly into his critical text” (p. 59); he finds the confidence with which Butterworth treats Jerome's account “mindboggling” (p. 60) and says Butterworth “uncritically accepts the view of Jerome as authoritative” (n. 46). other_findings.claim: The Greek of Against Celsus 6.26 and 8.72 and of Homilies on Jeremiah 20.3-4 was compared letter for letter, with accents, against the First1KGreek TEI transcriptions (Koetschau, GCS 2-3, for Against Celsus; Klostermann, GCS 6, for the homilies). For Against Celsus 6.26 a second, independent text (bkv.unifr.ch) agrees throughout (it prints ἄν for ἂν); for 8.72 it was compared on three clauses; for the homily no second text was found. The only differences from the transcriptions are a typing slip mended in each of 6.26 (πολῶν) and the homily (πρότρον), the angle brackets that mark the supplement ⟨ἐν⟩ at 8.72, and the quotation marks. The Greek of 8.72 has no word meaning ‘perhaps’: it sets aside whether evil could arise again as beyond the present purpose of the work.

The sources do not date the anathemas alike: Heide places the fifteen anathemas at the Council of Constantinople of AD 553, while the Catholic Encyclopedia article (Batiffol, 1907) says the doctrine was condemned in the first of the anathemas “at the Council of Constantinople in 543” and cites Justinian's Liber adversus Origenem, anathemas 7 and 9. This entry dates Justinian's Letter to Menas to 543 and calls the later list the ‘553 anathemas’, as Heide does; the dates were not checked against a primary source.

unverified: Koetschau's critical text of On First Principles (GCS 22, 1913) could not be read in sections; archive.org was reachable only through a tool that returns the first 59,000 characters or so. All Latin of On First Principles and of the Romans commentary is Migne's (Patrologia Graeca 11 and 14, Delarue's text) from OCR page images, so every status V on those passages means ‘checked against that printed edition’, not against Koetschau, Hammond Bammel, Crouzel-Simonetti or Behr. Spelling and some readings may differ there.

OCR gaps: On First Principles 3.6.5 (the destruction of the last enemy as the end of its hostile will, not its substance) was not obtained, nor the middle of Rufinus's Latin at 3.6.2-3, and one stretch of the Latin on the 1.2.13 page remains open (marked in the entry). Ramelli's use of 3.6.5 is known only through her review of Arruzza.
Justinian's Letter to Menas itself (PG 86.1, Mansi 9) was not opened; the Greek at 1.2.13 and 3.6.3 is as Migne prints it in PG 11, and was not checked against the letter.

English renderings are my own throughout. Crombie's public-domain English (ANF 4) was compared only for Against Celsus 6.26 and 8.72, through bkv.unifr.ch; elsewhere it is named and was not opened, and no public-domain English exists for the Romans commentary or the Jeremiah homilies as far as I know.

The readings for the Commentary on Romans 5.10 are partly about the problem the passage answers (freedom and certainty), not about 5.10 by name, and say so; Kimel's note quotes the passage without a location, and I matched it. For 6.5 no scholar who reads Origen's aionios as endless was read directly; McClymond's Jude 6 objection and the passage's own sentences are the nearest.

Most scholars were read through a web fetch tool that returns segmented summaries with short quotations (Martens, Heide twice, McClymond, Sytsma, Hannen, Nemes, Cavadini, Batiffol, Kimel, Ramelli's review of Arruzza, Somos), so their statuses are S, not V. balance_note: The draft heard mostly one voice on several passages (Ramelli's, Hannen's and Heide's restoration readings), and on the Homilies on Jeremiah 20 no one. Added or corrected in this pass: Martens on the Preface as the rule of faith; Hannen reporting Crouzel on 'research theology' and on 1.6; Batiffol on the caution of 2.10 and Against Celsus 6.26 (Origen 'at times reluctant to decide', not wishing the doctrine preached to all); Ramelli's own first-hand reading of 3.6.5 and 8.72 in her review of Arruzza; Somos on the Jeremiah homily; Heide's quotation of Crouzel on the ambiguity of aionios and McClymond's partial rejection of Ramelli's argument (Jude 6) for Romans 6.5; and the sentence of Romans 6.5 in which 'aeternus' is applied to the lost, which the draft had left out. Misattributions removed: a quotation from Origen put into Crouzel's mouth (1.6); a Crouzel citation in Heide placed under 2.10 instead of the aionios passage; Greggs credited with audience as well as genre; 'Joseph' Heine; Heide's 'perhaps' dropped; Heide's 'II to VI' given as 'II and VI'; the draft's gloss of McClymond ('partly meritorious', 'not as a proof of universalism'); and the Kimel note read as being about free will. The balance is still uneven. The readings of 5.10 and 6.5 are mostly about the general problem of aionios and freedom, not about the passage by name; for 6.5 the 'endless' side is carried by McClymond's objection and by the passage's own sentences, since no scholar of that view was read directly; and the Jeremiah homily has one reading. The hostile ancient readers (Jerome, and Justinian through the Greek fragments) are represented. The editors' split is reported by Martens in a review article and criticised by Cavadini and Heide, both of whom favour the Rufinus-printing side; no defender of Koetschau's method was read, and the editors' own reasons are heard only through those three.
